title: Cache shadowing and memory-channel overlap analysis
content:
Summary:

This note captures an exploratory investigation into a phenomenon we observed in recent load tests: transient latency spikes coincident with elevated memory-bandwidth utilization and increased KV-cache eviction churn. The working hypothesis is that 'cache shadowing' — overlapping accesses to nearby KV pages across memory channels — increases cross-channel contention and causes higher page migration/eviction rates under certain request mixes.

Goals:
- Measure whether KV access locality patterns can cause memory-channel overlap and measurable BW contention.
- Correlate eviction events with tail latency and noisy neighbors on the same NUMA node.
- Try low-effort mitigations (stride-aware prefetcher tuning, eviction hysteresis, small-set hot pinning) and capture signal.

Environment / baseline:
- Cluster: 4x GPU nodes (A100 40GB), dual-socket 64-core (AMD), 8 memory channels per CPU, huge pages enabled.
- Runtime: serving-runtime v1.18.2 (local branch: kv-shadowing-exp).
- KV store: per-model sharded in DRAM with slab allocator, default TTL=30s, page-size=4KB, page-grouping by 2MB region for numa placement.
- Workload: mixed small-chat (seq_len=64) + long-stream (seq_len=2048) at 1500 qps aggregate. Synthetic trace created from sampled production prefixes.
- Observability: nvidia-smi, sar, perf, msr-tools, meminfo sampling, and lightweight telemetry hooks in runtime to emit eviction_count, reuse_counter, page_faults per second.

Data collected (representative):
- 2024-02-22 14:24 baseline run (no mitigations)
  - avg latency: 23 ms
  - p95 latency: 62 ms
  - p99 latency: 310 ms (bursts)
  - KV reuse rate (per request): 0.28
  - Evictions/sec (node): 420
  - DRAM BW (read): 81 GB/s (peaks to 110 GB/s during bursts)
  - Page faults (minor/second): 0.9

- 2024-02-24 experiment with stride-aware prefetch disabled
  - avg latency: 24 ms
  - p95 latency: 70 ms
  - p99 latency: 420 ms
  - KV reuse rate: 0.25
  - Evictions/sec: 600
  - DRAM BW (read): 98 GB/s (peaks 135 GB/s)

- 2024-02-26 experiment with eviction hysteresis (+30% reuse threshold)
  - avg latency: 22 ms
  - p95 latency: 58 ms
  - p99 latency: 210 ms
  - KV reuse rate: 0.31
  - Evictions/sec: 260
  - DRAM BW (read): 76 GB/s (peaks 92 GB/s)

Initial observations:
- High eviction churn correlates strongly with p99 spikes and DRAM BW peaks.
- Disabling prefetch made things worse: lower reuse and more evictions. Hypothesis: prefetcher reduces long-tail misses when access order is somewhat predictable; turning it off increases random misses that stress the allocator.
- Eviction hysteresis (require reuse score decay before evict) reduced churn and brought p99 down substantially. It increased average memory residency of hot items and reduced page-scan thrash.
- Minor page faults are low, indicating most work is in-memory — the problem is bandwidth and local networked page-migrations rather than disk-backed paging.

Profiling notes and commands used:
- perf record -a -g -F 99 -- sleep 60 (sampled while load generator running) to capture kernel-side stalls.
- perf top and perf report to find page-fault related hotspots.
- likwid-perfctr to measure memory-channel utilization per socket.
- nsys profile for GPU-CPU interaction traces for long-sequence requests.
- runtime telemetry: /metrics/kv/evictions_total, /metrics/kv/reuse_histogram, and internal per-shard mem_bw counters emitted every 5s.

Microbench experiments to isolate channel overlap:
1) Synthetic stride test: generate access streams targeting addresses mapping to a single channel vs. alternating channels. Result: alternating channels increased observed channel-level queue latency and harmed throughput at high RPS.
2) Hotset clustering: cluster top-5% keys to same slab region vs. spread across regions. Clustering reduced BW but increased eviction pressure in that region; spreading improved p99 under moderate load.
3) Small-object pinning: reserve a tiny contiguous pool to pin hottest objects (manual mark) — reduced evictions by ~35% and p99 by ~40% on short runs.

Detailed hypothesis (sketch):
- When request mix contains interleaved long and short sequences, long sequences touch deep KV slices repeatedly (high reuse) while many short sequences introduce scattered one-off accesses. If allocator groups small pages into the same 2MB region without consideration of channel mapping, the combined pattern leads to bursts that saturate one or two memory channels and force cross-channel DMA and remote page placements (NUMA migration). This manifests as higher read BW on a subset of channels, increased eviction churn (because the local slab sees thrash), and long tail latency when those channels stall.

Proposed mitigations to test next (ordered):
- Make allocator channel-aware: prefer distributing new hot-region allocations round-robin across channels to avoid co-locating many hot sets on one channel.
- Adaptive hysteresis: tie eviction thresholds to observed local BW; increase hysteresis when BW > 85% sustained.
- Lightweight pinning policy: automatically detect top-k hot keys every 10s and pin to a protected pool; experiment with pool size 0.5%/1%/2% of memory.
- Prefetch tuning: keep prefetch enabled but limit its fanout to reduce speculative BW when patterns are noisy.
- Placement-aware sharding: adjust per-request shard selection to consider current per-shard BW load (cheap heuristic).

Open action items and experiments to run (with owners):
- Implement channel-aware allocator prototype in allocator/slot-manager: Evan (ETA 2w).
- Run long 12-hour stability run with hysteresis enabled to observe long-tail behavior: Priya (ETA 1w).
- Add lightweight hot-key detector to runtime telemetry (emit top-100 keys every 10s): Liam (ETA 1w).
- Instrument memory channel counters aggregated per-shard and send to console dashboards: Asha (ETA 4 days).

Notes / questions for further discussion:
- How sensitive are results to 2MB region grouping? Try varying the grouping granularity (keep both 2MB and 1GB hugepage grouping) and observe.
- Can we avoid per-request shard flips that cause cross-shard interleaving for long requests?
- Is there any existing kernel-level tunable (e.g., mem_interleave settings) we can tweak in operator-managed Dedicated environments?
- Are there specific customer workloads that would be negatively impacted by hysteresis (memory usage spikes)? Need to evaluate unit economics of added memory residency vs. token cost.

Appendix: quick commands and small scripts used:
- Measure per-channel bandwidth with likwid: likwid-perfctr -C 0-63 -g MEM -- sleep 20
- Small runner to create alternating-stride address touches (used to validate channel overlap): ./tools/stride-touch --base 0x7f0000000000 --stride 0x2000 --count 100000
- Telemetry snippet (prometheus style):
  kv_evictions_total{shard="s3"} 421
  kv_reuse_rate{shard="s3"} 0.28

Conclusion (working):
Cache shadowing is plausible and seems to materially affect p99 via bandwidth-channel hotspots and eviction churn. Early low-cost mitigations (eviction hysteresis, small-object pinning) show signal. The next step is a focused allocator change (channel-aware placement) and larger overnight runs to validate at scale.

If you want to pick this up: start with the hysteresis long run and the hot-key detector (Priya/Liam), then integrate results into the allocator prototype iteration.

Other context links: see linked_artifacts list above; add any additional GH issues back into JIRA-INF-2345.

End of note.
